title: Earth's Building Blocks Came from Next Door, Not the Outer Solar System
summary: For decades, planetary scientists have argued about where Earth's raw material came from. Many thought 6 to 40 percent of it drifted in from the outer solar system, beyond Jupiter — a handy explanation for how Earth got water and other volatile substances. A new study in Nature Astronomy says that idea is wrong. Paolo Sossi and Dan Bower of ETH Zurich compared isotope ratios from a wide range of meteorites — including samples linked to Mars and the asteroid Vesta — with Earth's own composition. Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different masses, like siblings who look alike but weigh different amounts. Earlier studies usually compared just two isotope systems. This team used ten. "Our studies are actually data science experiments," Sossi says. The result: Earth is made entirely of non-carbonaceous material, the kind that formed in the inner solar system. Outer-solar-system material makes up less than 2 percent of Earth's mass — possibly zero. "We were truly astonished," Bower says. The finding suggests Earth grew in a relatively stable environment, slowly collecting nearby planetary bodies. It also means water and other volatiles were probably already present in the inner solar system, not delivered from far away. Why the split? Jupiter likely acted as a barrier. As the gas giant grew, its gravity carved a gap in the protoplanetary disc — the ring of gas and dust where planets are born — limiting how much outer material could drift inward. Until now, scientists didn't know how effective that barrier was. Next, the team wants to keep testing the idea with more data.
why_it_matters: This rewrites a basic story about our own planet: if Earth's water and other light materials formed locally instead of arriving from the icy outer solar system, then rocky planets around other stars may also be born with the ingredients for oceans much closer to home than scientists assumed.

background_read: ETH Zurich, where Paolo Sossi and Dan Bower work, is a research university in Switzerland, and Nature Astronomy is a science journal where astronomers and planetary scientists publish their results.

Meteorites come in two broad chemical families: carbon-rich ones that formed far from the Sun, and the non-carbonaceous kind that formed in the warmer inner solar system. Scientists discovered this split by measuring isotopes, the heavy and light versions of the same atom.

Jupiter is the largest planet in the solar system, and scientists have long suspected that its gravity shaped the young solar system by blocking material from drifting inward. The asteroid Vesta, also mentioned in the study, is one of the biggest objects in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, and pieces of it have reached Earth as meteorites.

For years, one popular way to explain Earth's oceans was that icy comets or asteroids from beyond Jupiter delivered water here. This study challenges that picture by arguing the ingredients for water were already available closer to the Sun.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — a cleaner model of Earth's formation
perspectives.description: Supporters see the ten-isotope comparison as a much stronger test than earlier two-isotope studies, and it gives planetary scientists a simpler picture: Earth grew steadily from nearby material, and water was available right here. It also suggests Earth-like planets elsewhere may not need lucky comet deliveries to get oceans.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — indirect evidence and a reversed conclusion
perspectives.description: Sceptics could point out that earlier studies using fewer isotope systems reached the opposite conclusion, so the team must show its larger dataset isn't introducing its own bias. Isotope comparisons are indirect, and small differences in meteorite samples or measurement methods can shift the answer.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral — one round in a long argument
perspectives.description: Planetary science often advances by duelling datasets, and this fits that pattern. The carbon-rich versus non-carbonaceous split among meteorites was already known; the real dispute is about proportions, and no single paper usually ends a debate of this size.

The team plans to test the idea with more data, and future work could combine meteorite chemistry with observations of planet-forming discs around other stars. If Jupiter-like giants commonly block outer material, that could shape how astronomers search for worlds with oceans.
